The triad of bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and failure to pass meconium by 48 hours strongly suggests high-grade or complete obstruction. Midgut volvulus is top differential due to its life-threatening nature, rapid progression, and classic presentation—including bilious emesis and distension—often without prior feeding tolerance; malrotation is nearly universal in neonates with volvulus. Hirschsprung disease (especially total colonic aganglionosis) presents similarly in the first days of life with functional obstruction, distension, and delayed meconium passage; though typically less acutely bilious than volvulus, it remains highly plausible. Meconium ileus is strongly associated with cystic fibrosis and manifests as inspissated meconium causing distal ileal obstruction, leading to bilious vomiting and failure to pass meconium; its prevalence in neonates with this triad is ~10–15%. Duodenal atresia often presents within 24–48 hours with bilious or non-bilious vomiting (though ~30% are bilious), abdominal distension, and may show double-bubble sign on X-ray; it is less likely to cause complete meconium failure unless complicated, but remains a key structural diagnosis. Early-onset necrotizing enterocolitis (occurring <72h in term infants) is rarer but reported in association with perinatal stressors or congenital infections; it can mimic obstruction with bilious vomiting, distension, and ileus, though systemic signs (apnea, lethargy, thrombocytopenia) are usually present—absence of specified systemic symptoms lowers but does not exclude it. Other diagnoses (e.g., jejunoileal atresia, annular pancreas) are less common and lack distinguishing features in this data."}
